# What survives without the authors' code? Reproducing thirteen economics and political-science papers with an LLM pipeline and an LLM agent

*First draft, 2026-10-23.  Every table between `<!-- table:… -->` markers is generated by `docs/report/tables.py` from the committed results files; re-run `uv run python docs/report/tables.py` to refresh them.  Numbers in the prose are copied from those tables or quoted from `ROADMAP.md` with the section named.*

> **Editor's note:** Title.  Alternatives: "Seeded, independent, blind: a reproduction benchmark for LLM agents on I4R-replicated papers"; "Translating the code versus reading the paper: what an LLM reproduces when the replication scripts are withheld."  The working title from the brief ("Reproducing economics and political-science results with an LLM: a benchmark of three reproduction modes, two harnesses, and the gap between them") is accurate but long.

## 1. Summary

We built a benchmark that asks a language-model system to reproduce the headline numbers of published economics and political-science papers, scored against the papers' printed values and against the values that human replicators at the Institute for Replication (I4R) obtained.  Each paper is attempted in three modes: *seeded* (the authors' replication scripts are provided), *independent* (scripts withheld, target values shown) and *blind* (scripts and target values withheld).  Two systems sat the benchmark: a fixed pipeline that writes one R script and refines it, and a Claude Code agent with its own loop.  On thirteen evaluation papers (154 pinned claims) the agent reproduced 153, 148 and 135 claims within tolerance of the paper's printed value in seeded, independent and blind mode.  The pipeline, run on the same model family, reproduced 149, 129 and 92.  On the seven papers where an older model was also run, moving the pipeline from `claude-opus-4-7` to Opus 5.5 raised its blind count from 24 to 51 of 79, against the agent's 75.  The finding: with the authors' code in hand both systems are near the ceiling, and the loss when the code and the targets are withheld is mostly a property of the harness and of what the papers' methods sections leave unstated.  The limitation: every cell is a single run on a corpus of thirteen papers that all predate the models' training cutoffs, so none of these differences carries a measured uncertainty.

## 2. Introduction

A replication package is a set of data files and the scripts that turn them into the paper's tables.  Re-running the scripts and checking that the printed numbers come out is *computational reproduction*.  It confirms that the package is complete and that the code does what the tables say, but the specification (which sample, which controls, which estimator, which standard errors) travels inside the scripts.  A replicator who rebuilds the analysis from the paper's text and the raw data, without the authors' code, performs a different test: whether the paper describes its own analysis well enough to be redone.  We call that *independent reproduction*.  A third variant withholds the printed results as well, so that the replicator cannot steer toward the known answer.  We call that *blind reproduction*.

The three are routinely reported under one word.  "The model reproduced the paper" can mean that it translated a Stata do-file into R, that it rebuilt the regression from the methods section while knowing the target coefficient, or that it derived the coefficient without ever seeing it.  These are different claims about the model and different claims about the paper.  This benchmark keeps them apart: every result row records its mode, and no number in this report pools two modes.

The ground truth comes from the Institute for Replication (I4R), which organizes replication games in which teams of economists and political scientists reproduce recently published papers and file reports.  I4R's first meta-database covers 110 replication reports on 109 papers from leading economics and political-science journals, with estimate-level rows that record both the paper's coefficient and the replicator's (`benchmark/corpus/SOURCE.md`).  It is the only source we know of that gives, for each paper, a human replicator's number to set beside the published one.  That matters for two of our papers, where the replicators found that the published numbers are wrong.

Two systems were evaluated.  The *pipeline* is a fixed program: it extracts the paper's text and a methodology summary, writes one R script with a language model, runs it in a sandbox, repairs it when it crashes (an *error refinement*), and, when the target values are shown, tells the model which claims are off and by how much and asks for a corrected script (a *claim refinement*), with at most three of each.  The *agent* is a Claude Code session given the same task text, the same data mount and the same sandbox, and left to run its own loop: it can inspect the data, run exploratory scripts, read the whole paper and try alternatives.  Both are scored by the same harness from the numbers their final script prints.  The question the comparison answers is how much of what looks like a model's reproduction ability is the loop around it.

> **Editor's note:** The intro does not yet position the work against I4R's own AI replication games or other LLM-replication benchmarks.  A paragraph with citations is needed here; I did not add references from memory.

## 3. The benchmark

### 3.1 Catalog

The catalog has eighteen entries, one YAML file per paper under `benchmark/papers/`.  Two are out of scope (one has no open-access full text, one has gated data), leaving sixteen: three *dev* papers used while building the pipeline and thirteen *evaluation* papers never used to tune it.  Twelve of the evaluation papers came from a shortlist drawn from the I4R meta-database on 2026-10-21 and checked against five requirements: not already cataloged, a public replication package downloadable without login, readable software and data formats, an open paper PDF, and an I4R verdict (`benchmark/corpus/candidates-2026-10-21.md`).  The shortlist was itself the end of a funnel: ROADMAP Phase 4 records that of 110 reports, 60 were machine-readable runnable candidates and only about nine R-runnable ones carried a public report link.  Selection was therefore by availability, not at random.

"Original software" is the language of the authors' package.  Every reproduction, whatever the original, is written in R and run in an R sandbox; Stata originals are in scope because the seeded prompt can show the do-file and because the claims can be checked without running Stata.  "I4R values" counts the pinned claims for which the replicators recorded their own number.  The I4R outcome label is the meta-database's verdict mapped onto the catalog schema; papers I4R rated "minor discrepancies" carry the label `reproducible` here.

### 3.2 Pinned claims

A *pinned claim* is one published number that the benchmark scores: a coefficient, a standard error, a test statistic or a sample size, stored with its printed value, its standard error where the paper gives one, a location ("Table 1, column 2") and a short description of what it is.  The curation rule (`benchmark/README.md`, "Curating headline claims") admits a number only if it is in the abstract or a main results table, the paper's conclusions rest on it, and it is stated numerically; the target is eight to twelve claims per paper.  The evaluation papers carry 154 pinned claims, the dev papers 35.

Each claim also has a *context* string, written in the paper's own words, which every mode shows to the reproducer.  Two curation rules came out of leaks found during the project.  Contexts may not name package variables, file names or commands (ROADMAP 1.7, where the first contexts had been written from the package), and no context may state the value of any pinned claim of its entry, which a catalog test now enforces (ROADMAP 3.4, PR #69).

### 3.3 Three modes

The modes differ only in what the reproducer is shown.

| Mode | Authors' scripts | Script-free data copy | Claim values and SEs | Claim refinement loop | What a pass measures |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| seeded | shown, as ground truth | no (full package) | shown | on | translating the authors' code |
| independent | withheld | yes | shown | on | rebuilding the analysis from the text, knowing the targets |
| blind | withheld | yes | withheld (also redacted from the paper text) | off | deriving the numbers without seeing them |

In independent and blind mode the data directory is a *script-free copy*: scripts are removed by file name, and logs, transcripts, code saved under other names and generated regression tables are removed by content (`benchmark/README.md`, "The script-free copy").  Blind mode additionally redacts every pinned value and standard error from the paper text, including percentage forms such as "3.5 points" for 0.035.  A blind pass is therefore the only count free of *target-guided search*, by which we mean changing the analysis until the printed number appears.

### 3.4 Tolerance and scoring

A claim *passes* when the reproduced value is within tolerance of the paper's printed value.  We report these as counts of claims, not as rates.  Seeded mode uses a strict relative band per claim type (2 % for coefficients, 5 % for standard errors, 1 % for other quantities such as sample sizes; `benchmark/README.md` and `src/retally/validation/comparator.py`), because translating the authors' code should land on their numbers.  Independent and blind mode accept a value within one standard error of the printed value when the claim pins a standard error, never narrower than the relative band, and use the relative band otherwise; rebuilding a specification from prose is not expected to hit the fourth decimal.  In every mode the band is never narrower than half a unit in the printed value's last decimal place, so a reproduction that rounds to the printed number always passes.  This floor matters for papers that print coefficients to one significant digit.

The wider independent band is a real asymmetry.  A pass count in independent mode is not comparable with one in seeded mode on closeness, so we report median relative error and the share of claims within one, two and five times their tolerance beside every count (Section 4.6).

Scoring belongs to the harness, not the reproducer.  The reproducer returns raw `name = value` pairs printed by its final script; the harness matches them to the pinned claims and applies the mode's tolerance.  Three verdicts are recorded per paper and never collapsed into one: `retally_ran` (the reproducer finished), `agrees_with_paper` (every pinned claim within tolerance of the printed value) and `agrees_with_i4r` (every claim for which I4R recorded a value, and for which the reproducer printed a value, within tolerance of the *replicator's* value).  A reproduction that matches the paper but not the replicators is the case the benchmark exists to surface.

Each row also records a *first-scored* count: the claims passed by the first execution that printed a parsable result, after any crash repairs and before any claim-targeted feedback.  The difference between first scored and final is what target-guided refinement added.

### 3.5 The `Reproducer` protocol and the two reproducers

The harness talks to a reproducer through one method, `reproduce(paper_source, language, dataset_reference, claims, reproduction_mode)`, which returns a `Reproduction`: the raw outputs keyed by claim name, the generated code, its output and exit code, declared deviations and per-stage flags, and no verdicts (`benchmark/reproducer.py`).  The pipeline is the reference implementation.  The agent is plugged in through a file-system reproducer: a rendering step writes a task directory (the pipeline generator's own claims block, dataset listing and mode instructions, the paper text, and the mode's data mount), a Claude Code subagent does the task and writes its scripts, outputs and a manifest, and the harness scores the files (ROADMAP 3.3).  The harness never drives the agent and never calls the API for it.

The agent's isolation is partly by instruction.  Its task directory holds only the mode's mount, and the sandbox mounts nothing else, but the session runs inside a checkout of this repository, where the catalog (with pinned values) and the download cache (with the authors' scripts) are readable.  Each agent had to list every file it read outside its mount; across the runs reported here the lists were empty or named only the task's own files (ROADMAP 3.3).

### 3.6 Models

Three model configurations appear, and the report never pools them.  The pipeline's original rows ran on `claude-opus-4-7` with no extended thinking (ROADMAP 3.5).  The pipeline was then moved to `claude-opus-5-5` through the API, with effort `high` for code generation and refinement and `medium` for claim extraction (`src/retally/llm.py`); credit allowed four of the seven earlier evaluation papers.  The agent rows, and the oracle rows below, ran on the Claude desktop app's Opus model at its default effort; the agents reported it as Opus 5.5.

### 3.7 The LLM oracle

The *oracle* runs the pipeline with every Claude call answered out of band rather than by the API (`src/retally/llm_oracle.py`, ROADMAP 3.5).  The pipeline's requests are built exactly as for a live run; each unanswered one is written to disk, a Claude Code subagent told to use no tools and read nothing but the prompt writes the answer, the answer is installed, and the run resumes.  It guarantees that the prompts, the loop and the scoring are the pipeline's own, that oracle answers live in a separate cache and can never be served to a real API run, and that oracle rows carry their own label.  It does not guarantee that the answerer thinks at the effort the request names (the subagents run at the desktop default), and it does not enforce isolation: two of 88 answering subagents reported running a harmless shell command on their own answer file, and none reported reading anything outside the prompt (ROADMAP 3.5).  The oracle let us run the remaining nine evaluation papers through the pipeline at no API cost.

### 3.8 Sandbox and cost accounting

Every script, from either reproducer, runs in the same Docker image (`retally-sandbox-r`, 47 R packages plus base; ROADMAP 1.8) with no network, a read-only file system and the pipeline executor's limits of 300 seconds, 4 GB and one CPU (ROADMAP 3.3).  Pipeline rows record the tokens each API call used, by model, and an estimated cost from one price table (`benchmark/pricing.py`).  Agent and oracle rows use plan usage, which the results files do not price.

## 4. Results

Read the modes separately.  Seeded numbers measure translation of the authors' code.  Independent numbers measure reconstruction from the text with the targets visible and a refinement loop chasing them.  Blind numbers are the only ones free of target-guided search.  Every cell is one run.

### 4.1 The pipeline on `claude-opus-4-7`

On the seven evaluation papers measured first, the pipeline on `claude-opus-4-7` reproduced 55 of 79 claims seeded, 41 independent and 24 blind.  Its first-scored counts were 46, 27 and 24.  Seeded was not a ceiling.  Grier failed in every mode, including seeded, because the model estimated a conditional logit instead of the paper's logit with fixed-effect dummies, and Arias passed only its four counts seeded because the model re-estimated the conjoint effects with a linear model instead of translating the package's `cjoint::amce` call (ROADMAP 3.2).  Montero is the clearest single case.  I4R found duplicated rows behind the paper's Table 5 earnings results.  Seeded, the first script matched neither the paper nor the replicators; one claim-refinement round, told the gaps to the printed values, then reproduced the paper's printed numbers exactly.  Target-guided search converged on numbers the replicators had shown to be wrong (ROADMAP 3.2).

### 4.2 The agent on thirteen papers

The agent reproduced 153, 148 and 135 of 154 claims seeded, independent and blind, with first-scored counts of 151, 146 and 128.  On the seven papers above it reached 78, 78 and 75 of 79.  Its misses are few and concentrated: in independent mode six claims on three papers, in blind mode nineteen on five (Section 5).  Two caveats belong next to these numbers.  First, the agent's first execution is usually a data-inspection run that prints nothing, so its *first-attempt* count is meaningless; first scored is the comparable figure.  Second, its error and claim refinement counts are its own bookkeeping, and ROADMAP 3.3 records two re-runs steered by numbers stated in claim contexts that were not labeled as claim refinements, so those counts are a lower bound.

### 4.3 The model confound and its resolution

The agent ran on a newer model than the pipeline's original rows, so the comparison in 4.1–4.2 mixes a model difference with a harness difference.  To separate them we ran the pipeline on Opus 5.5: through the API for four papers (Grier, Leeson, Manekin, Montero) and through the oracle for the other three (Adams, Arias, Hanlon).

### 4.4 Decomposing the gap

On the seven papers that have all three rows, the difference between the agent and the original pipeline splits exactly into a model effect (pipeline on Opus 5.5 minus pipeline on 4.7) and a harness effect (agent minus pipeline on Opus 5.5).

<!-- table:gap_decomposition -->
Differences in claims within tolerance, summed over papers.  On the 3.2 set the total agent-over-pipeline-4.7 difference splits exactly into a model effect (pipeline on Opus 5.5 minus pipeline on 4.7) and a harness effect (agent minus pipeline on Opus 5.5).  The 3.4 papers have no 4.7 rows, so only the harness effect exists there.  One run per cell; no uncertainty is attached to any difference.

| Papers | Mode | Claims | Agent − pipeline 4.7 | Model effect (5.5 − 4.7) | Harness effect (agent − 5.5) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 papers (3.2 set) | seeded | 79 | +23 | +24 | -1 |
| 7 papers (3.2 set) | independent | 79 | +37 | +26 | +11 |
| 7 papers (3.2 set) | blind | 79 | +51 | +27 | +24 |
| API route (4) | seeded | 44 | +15 | +16 | -1 |
| API route (4) | independent | 44 | +19 | +9 | +10 |
| API route (4) | blind | 44 | +33 | +10 | +23 |
| oracle route (3) | seeded | 35 | +8 | +8 | +0 |
| oracle route (3) | independent | 35 | +18 | +17 | +1 |
| oracle route (3) | blind | 35 | +18 | +17 | +1 |
| 6 papers (3.4 set) | seeded | 75 | — | — | +5 |
| 6 papers (3.4 set) | independent | 75 | — | — | +8 |
| 6 papers (3.4 set) | blind | 75 | — | — | +19 |
| all 13 | seeded | 154 | — | — | +4 |
| all 13 | independent | 154 | — | — | +19 |
| all 13 | blind | 154 | — | — | +43 |
<!-- /table:gap_decomposition -->

On the seven papers the model effect is roughly constant across modes (24, 26 and 27 claims), while the harness effect is about zero in seeded mode (−1) and grows as more is withheld (11 claims independent, 24 blind).  The reading in ROADMAP 3.5 follows from this: once the authors' code is gone, the agent's ability to look at the data and try alternatives is worth more, and more again once the targets are gone too.  On the six later papers, where only the harness effect exists, it is 5, 8 and 19 claims.[^six-gap]

This decomposition should not be leaned on hard, for three reasons.  The four API papers were chosen, when credit allowed only four, by the size of the agent-over-pipeline gap per dollar (ROADMAP 3.5); they lean toward papers where the original pipeline did badly.  The route split shows the consequence: almost all of the seven-paper harness effect comes from the API route (10 claims independent, 23 blind), while on the three oracle-route papers it is one claim in each of those modes.  Second, the two halves of "pipeline on Opus 5.5" are not the same answerer: the API rows run at named effort levels, the oracle rows at the desktop default.  Third, with one run per cell and the run-to-run spread shown in Section 4.8, none of these differences has a standard error, and we make no claim of statistical significance for any of them.

> **Editor's note:** How hard to lean on the model-versus-harness decomposition is a judgment call.  The defensible core is the seven-paper total and the qualitative pattern (harness effect zero seeded, larger blind).  The per-route split argues for caution, because the route was confounded with paper selection.  Options: present the decomposition as the main result with the caveats above (current draft), demote it to a paragraph, or spend roughly $10–13 (ROADMAP 3.5) on an API run of the nine oracle papers to remove the effort caveat before leaning on it.

### 4.5 What refinement buys

<!-- table:refinement -->
*First attempt* is the very first execution, crash or not; *first scored* is the first execution that printed a parsable `RESULT:` line (after crash repairs, before any claim-targeted feedback).  The agent's first execution is usually a data-inspection run, so its first-attempt count is not reported.  Blind mode runs no claim refinements by construction.

| Reproducer | Papers | Mode | Final | First scored | First attempt | Final − first scored | Error refinements | Claim refinements | Cells with a claim refinement |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Pipeline, `claude-opus-4-7` | 7 | seeded | 55 / 79 | 46 | 34 | +9 | 2 | 6 | 4 / 7 |
| Pipeline, `claude-opus-4-7` | 7 | independent | 41 / 79 | 27 | 19 | +14 | 10 | 12 | 6 / 7 |
| Pipeline, `claude-opus-4-7` | 7 | blind | 24 / 79 | 24 | 10 | +0 | 5 | 0 | 0 / 7 |
| Pipeline, `claude-opus-5-5` (API) | 4 | seeded | 44 / 44 | 43 | 43 | +1 | 0 | 3 | 1 / 4 |
| Pipeline, `claude-opus-5-5` (API) | 4 | independent | 33 / 44 | 21 | 20 | +12 | 3 | 4 | 3 / 4 |
| Pipeline, `claude-opus-5-5` (API) | 4 | blind | 20 / 44 | 20 | 20 | +0 | 0 | 0 | 0 / 4 |
| Pipeline, desktop Opus (oracle) | 9 | seeded | 105 / 110 | 105 | 105 | +0 | 0 | 2 | 1 / 9 |
| Pipeline, desktop Opus (oracle) | 9 | independent | 96 / 110 | 68 | 68 | +28 | 0 | 16 | 6 / 9 |
| Pipeline, desktop Opus (oracle) | 9 | blind | 72 / 110 | 72 | 65 | +0 | 1 | 0 | 0 / 9 |
| Agent (Claude Code, desktop Opus) | 13 | seeded | 153 / 154 | 151 | n/a | +2 | 3 | 1 | 1 / 13 |
| Agent (Claude Code, desktop Opus) | 13 | independent | 148 / 154 | 146 | n/a | +2 | 0 | 6 | 5 / 13 |
| Agent (Claude Code, desktop Opus) | 13 | blind | 135 / 154 | 128 | n/a | +7 | 2 | 0 | 0 / 13 |
<!-- /table:refinement -->

In independent mode the refinement loop accounts for a large share of the pipeline's passes: 14 of its 41 claims on `claude-opus-4-7`, 12 of 33 on the API run and 28 of 96 on the oracle run come after the first scored script, through claim refinements in most cells.  For the agent the same difference is 2 of 148.  In seeded mode refinement adds little to any configuration on Opus 5.5.  In blind mode there are no claim refinements by construction, so the pipeline's final and first-scored counts are equal; the agent's blind count rises from 128 first scored to 135 final without any claim refinement, because it re-ran scripts after checking them against the paper's definitions (Hanlon's spline terms, ROADMAP 3.3) and, in two cells, against counts stated in claim contexts before that leak was closed (ROADMAP 3.3).  The pipeline's independent passes are therefore a mix of derivation and search, and the agent's are mostly derivation.  This is the reason to headline blind and first-scored counts rather than final independent counts.

Pass counts saturate and hide how far off a miss is.  On the seven-paper set the pipeline on `claude-opus-4-7` had a median relative error of 22.3 % in blind mode, with only 51 % of matched claims within five times their tolerance; on Opus 5.5 the same papers give 1.3 % and 71 %, and the agent 0.3 % and 96 %.  Two cautions apply.  The independent and blind band is one standard error, which for imprecise estimates is wide: the agent's Montero independent and blind values pass at relative errors of 23–36 % (ROADMAP 3.3).  And "matched" means that a value was printed under the claim's name; claims printed as missing are excluded from the error statistics and counted in the match rate.

The cell the benchmark was designed to find, a reproduction that agrees with the replicators and not with the paper, did not occur in a substantive form.[^i4r-cell]  The table does show four rows in that column, but each is an artifact of how the I4R verdict is defined: it is computed over the claims that have an I4R value *and* a printed reproduction.  The agent's three Grier rows each miss one claim for which I4R recorded no value, and the Manekin blind row on `claude-opus-4-7` printed no value for the six claims it missed.

The two papers I4R rated not reproducible tell the more useful story.  On Montero, every configuration in seeded mode reproduced the paper's printed numbers, which the replicators showed are produced by duplicated rows; the seeded agent did so on its first script by following the do-file's "replicating original results" block (ROADMAP 3.3).  Seeded reproduction faithfully reproduces a package's error.  Independent and blind agents built a paper-faithful specification that matched neither the paper (except inside the wide band) nor the replicators.  Holman shows the same pattern: seeded runs follow the do-file, which estimates random effects and a linear model where the paper says fixed effects and a logit, and reproduce the printed numbers that I4R's report (DP41) corrected; the blind agent did what the paper says and reproduced neither (ROADMAP 3.4).

Variance has been measured in two places only.  On the dev papers the pipeline on `claude-opus-4-7` was run in independent mode once with the LLM call cache on and three times with it off.  The spread is wide where the paper is hard: Alesina ranged from 0 to 7 of 11 across four runs, Bisbee from 5 to 8; Dincecco, once its file-selection problem was fixed, was 13 of 13 in all three fresh runs.  The agent was re-run in blind mode on five papers.  Adams and Arias repeated exactly; Grier, Gagliarducci and Holman moved by one or two claims, and ROADMAP 3.4 reports that in each case the miss itself was stable (the same paper-versus-code issue both times) while borderline claims crossed the band.  Every other cell in this report, including every pipeline-on-Opus-5.5 cell, is a single run.  The planned design (Phase 5) is three runs per paper per mode on a frozen harness; until that exists, a difference of a few claims between two cells should be read as noise.

The two token figures are not comparable (the oracle starts a fresh subagent for every pipeline call), and we have no like-for-like dollar figure for either.

## 5. Failure taxonomy

We classified every claim that missed in independent or blind mode on the evaluation papers, for the pipeline on `claude-opus-4-7` (seven papers), the pipeline on Opus 5.5 (thirteen papers: API rows where they exist, oracle rows otherwise) and the agent (thirteen papers).  The classification rests on the per-paper analyses in ROADMAP 3.2–3.5 and the claimed and reproduced values in the results files; each rule, with the passage it relies on, is in `TAXONOMY_RULES` in `docs/report/tables.py`, and the per-claim list is in `docs/report/tables/taxonomy_claims.md`.  A claim is classified by the root cause ROADMAP gives for its row; where ROADMAP gives none, it is unclassified.

<!-- table:taxonomy -->
Pipeline 4.7: the seven 3.2 papers.  Pipeline 5.5: all thirteen evaluation papers (API rows for Grier, Leeson, Manekin and Montero; oracle rows for the other nine).  Agent: all thirteen.

| Category | pipeline 4.7, independent | pipeline 4.7, blind | pipeline 5.5, independent | pipeline 5.5, blind | agent, independent | agent, blind | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| data-file resolution | 0 | 0 | 11 | 12 | 0 | 0 | 23 |
| specification mismatch | 0 | 19 | 6 | 6 | 0 | 6 | 37 |
| sample restriction | 5 | 11 | 0 | 21 | 0 | 0 | 37 |
| SE / cluster choice | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| tolerance artifact | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| extraction error | 12 | 8 | 0 | 6 | 0 | 0 | 26 |
| under-specified methods section | 3 | 8 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 13 | 37 |
| unclassified | 18 | 9 | 4 | 13 | 0 | 0 | 44 |
| **all misses** | 38 | 55 | 25 | 62 | 6 | 19 | 205 |
| claims scored | 79 | 79 | 154 | 154 | 154 | 154 | 774 |
<!-- /table:taxonomy -->

**Data-file resolution.**  The reproducer read the wrong file.  On Montero blind the pipeline on Opus 5.5 built its regression on 130 rows instead of 4,770 because it never found the right data file without the scripts (ROADMAP 3.5).  On Grier the package ships three datasets that differ only in the contribution window and never says which is which; the pipeline landed on 172 and 94 observations instead of 186 and 106, while the agent resolved the ambiguity by trying both files (ROADMAP 3.4–3.5).  Every miss in this category belongs to the pipeline.

**Specification mismatch.**  The reproducer estimated a different model from the one the paper states.  The pipeline on `claude-opus-4-7` produced every Adams blind coefficient with the wrong sign (ROADMAP 3.2).  The oracle pipeline fitted random-effects and linear-probability models on Holman where the paper specifies fixed effects and a logit (ROADMAP 3.5).  Because the authors' code also uses random effects and a linear model (ROADMAP 3.4), that description cannot be the whole explanation of the Holman misses; those cells need a closer look before publication.  The agent's six specification misses are all Gagliarducci blind: it used the dataset's percent-opposite variable, which is missing for bills with no cosponsors, where the paper divides by cosponsors plus one, so Panel B lost bills and its coefficients moved (ROADMAP 3.4).

**Sample restriction.**  The model was right and the sample was not.  The oracle pipeline ran Altmann blind on 17,840 observations instead of 12,160 by taking the wrong subset of treatment arms, and Acemoglu blind on 178 and 171 clusters instead of 181 and 175 (ROADMAP 3.5).  On Leeson blind the pipeline on Opus 5.5 got the five-station subsample wrong (98 visits against 102), and with it the two dollars-per-hour tests (ROADMAP 3.5); the run on `claude-opus-4-7` also missed both visit counts (ROADMAP 3.2).

**SE or cluster choice.**  No evaluation-paper miss in independent or blind mode was attributed to the standard-error or clustering choice.  The category is not empty in the project: on the dev paper Dincecco, two standard-error claims failed because the generated code used HC1 where Stata's `ivreg2, r` reports HC0 (ROADMAP 1.7–1.8).

**Tolerance artifact.**  One miss.  The agent's independent Grier run gives −0.000565 for a coefficient the paper prints as −0.0005; the authors' own script gives the same value, so the printed digit is itself off by 12.9 % against a 10 % band (ROADMAP 3.3).  The opposite artifact, passes the band lets through, is more consequential and is discussed in Section 4.6.

**Extraction error.**  No usable value reached the scorer: the script crashed, printed `NA`, or printed results under other names.  All of these are pipeline misses.  The pipeline on `claude-opus-4-7` printed nothing on Grier independent after three error repairs and `NA` for all six Study 1 coefficients on Manekin blind (ROADMAP 3.2).

**Under-specified methods section.**  The paper's text does not determine the number, or states a rule the authors' code does not follow, so a reproducer that follows the text misses and the seeded run, following the code, does not.  This is the category the benchmark exists to measure, and it accounts for 18 of the agent's 25 misses.  López-Moctezuma's four attitude-index effects fail in independent and blind mode for both harnesses because the paper does not state the attendance weights or the item orientations (ROADMAP 3.4).  Adams states that both parties need at least four MPs; the authors filtered on one party only, and the blind agent, applying the stated rule twice, got 1,535 dyads against 1,842 both times (ROADMAP 3.3–3.4).  Montero's paper states a five-member rule its code never applied (ROADMAP 3.2), and Holman's states fixed effects and a logit where its code uses random effects and a linear model (ROADMAP 3.4).  Grier's deflator base year is unstated; two agent runs chose different years, which rescales every contribution coefficient by 8 % (ROADMAP 3.3).

**Unclassified.**  Forty-four misses, all of them the pipeline's, have no stated cause in ROADMAP, among them the Arias independent conjoint effects on `claude-opus-4-7`, the Montero independent misses on `claude-opus-4-7` and several single-claim misses on the oracle rows.  The Grier blind coefficients are left unclassified deliberately: the rows on `claude-opus-4-7` and on Opus 5.5 print identical coefficients to every digit, and ROADMAP attributes the first to the estimator (3.2) and the second to the data file (3.5).  Both cannot be the whole story.

> **Editor's note:** The Phase 5 category list has no slot for "the paper's text and the authors' code disagree".  I put those cases (Adams, Montero, Holman) under "under-specified methods section", since a reader of the text cannot recover the published number.  Splitting them into their own category would make the finding about the literature sharper.  Your call.

> **Editor's note:** Naming papers whose methods sections do not determine their own numbers is a statement about named authors.  Phase 0 of the roadmap removed a leaderboard for that reason.  Consider whether the per-paper examples in this section should stay named in the public version, and whether to contact the authors first.

## 6. Limitations

**Contamination.**  Every paper predates every evaluated model's training data.  The corpus is drawn from 2022–2023 replication games, and ROADMAP's north star notes that current model training cutoffs extend into 2026.  The first public versions of the sixteen in-scope papers date from 2015-08 to 2022-06-14 and their packages from 2020-08-27 to 2023-03-31.

We therefore cannot populate a pre-cutoff versus post-cutoff split, and we do not offer one.  A model may have seen a paper, its package or its I4R report.  The gap between modes is conditional on whatever the model already knows; it is not a contamination control.  The cheap memorization probe planned in Phase 5 (ask for a paper's headline coefficient with no data access) has not been run.

**Seeded and independent mode show the targets.**  Only blind mode withholds the printed values.  Independent passes include target-guided search (Section 4.5).

**Remaining leaks.**  The dataset listing's row counts equal a pinned sample size for Acemoglu (5,775) and López-Moctezuma (39), and a rounded prose value survives blind redaction on Holman ("3.1 points" for 3.112); both affect the pipeline and the agent identically (ROADMAP 3.4).  Claim contexts stated sample sizes for Adams, Leeson and Montero until PR #69 moved them to the entries' notes; the agent rows for the first seven papers (ROADMAP 3.3) predate that fix, and two blind agents used those counts (ROADMAP 3.3).  The agent's refinement counts are self-reported.  The agent's isolation from the repository checkout is by instruction and by its own report of files read.

**The oracle is not the API.**  Oracle answers come from desktop subagents at default effort, not at the effort the pipeline's request names; isolation is by instruction; and the extraction prompts truncate the paper text by design, which several answering agents noted (ROADMAP 3.5).  We present oracle rows beside the API rows, labeled, and never pool them in a table.  The "pipeline on Opus 5.5" aggregate in Sections 4.3–4.4 combines the two routes by paper, and its caveats are stated there.

**One run per cell.**  See Section 4.8.

**Scope.**  Every reproduction is written in R.  Stata originals are included only because their claims can be scored without running Stata.  The corpus is thirteen evaluation papers (154 claims), selected by availability of open data, open PDFs and an I4R verdict, not at random; five of the thirteen are from APSR or AJPS, and most methods are regressions on observational or experimental data.

**Tolerance choices.**  The seeded band is strict; the independent and blind band is one standard error and can pass values a quarter or more away from the printed number when the estimate is imprecise.  Changing either moves the counts.

**Seeded mode reproduces the package's mistakes.**  Montero seeded passes every claim on every configuration, and the numbers it reproduces are wrong (Section 4.7).  A seeded pass certifies the package, not the paper's result.

## 7. Using the benchmark with another agent

Any system that implements the `Reproducer` protocol can be scored on the same catalog without changing the harness.  It receives the paper source, the target language, a reference to the dataset, the pinned claims and the mode, and returns raw outputs keyed by claim name plus its code and logs.  The harness, not the agent, applies the tolerance and records the three verdicts, so no reproducer can grade its own exam or narrow the claim set.  An adapter must honor the mode by what is on disk (the script-free copy in independent and blind mode, not an instruction alone), run its code in the same network-less sandbox image, and raise rather than return junk when it cannot produce a result (`benchmark/README.md`, "Plugging in another agent").  A reproducer is registered by name in `benchmark/runner.py` or passed as `module:factory` on the command line.

The agent in this report used the file-system route: render a task per cell, let the agent work, score the files it leaves.  That route needs no code changes for a new agent, only a session that follows `task.md`.  The I4R meta-database the catalog draws on is MIT-licensed (`benchmark/corpus/SOURCE.md`).  The repository itself carries no license file, so the license of the catalog, the pinned claims and the harness is currently unstated.

> **Editor's note:** Choose a license before release (for example MIT or Apache-2.0 for code, CC BY 4.0 for the catalog and pinned claims).  The report should state it here.

## 8. Next steps

Four pieces of work would most change what this report can claim.  A variance pass, three runs per paper per mode on a frozen and tagged harness, would let the gaps carry uncertainty.  Corpus growth to the 20–30 papers the roadmap targets, with the open-data and open-PDF funnel recorded, would make the per-category counts in Section 5 mean something.  The memorization probe would put a number on contamination.  And the pipeline freeze question needs an answer: the two Opus 5.5 pipeline misses that are harness rather than model (Grier's window file, Montero blind's data file) are concrete targets if tuning is unfrozen, but tuning on evaluation papers would end their use as evaluation papers.

> **Editor's note:** Venue.  Options in ROADMAP Phase 5: an arXiv or SocArXiv preprint, the I4R discussion-paper series (I4R has run AI replication games and is the natural audience), or a methods journal.  The register of this draft fits the first two.
